keyVerseText: But I trust in the Lord Jesus to send Timotheus shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state. But: or, Moreover
rootMeaning: The Greek verb εὐψυχέω (eupsychéō) comes from a compound of εὖ (eû), meaning 'good' or 'well,' and ψυχή (psychḗ), meaning 'soul' or 'life.' Literally, it conveys the idea of having a 'good soul' or being 'well-spirited,' which extends beyond mere external comfort to an inward state of courage and encouragement. This etymology enriches the common English gloss 'be of good comfort' by emphasizing a deep, soulful well-being and moral strength.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Philippians 2:19, where it is translated as 'may be of good comfort.' Despite its rarity, the consistency in translation highlights its core meaning of encouragement and good spirits. The limited occurrence suggests it was a specialized term used to express heartfelt encouragement, especially in personal and pastoral contexts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding εὐψυχέω as 'being of good courage' or 'encouraged in spirit' is significant for Christian faith because it captures the essence of hope and inner strength that believers are called to embody. Rooted in the goodness of the soul, this word reminds us that Christian comfort is not superficial but grounded in the well-being that comes from trust in God. It encourages believers to maintain courage and encouragement even amid trials, reflecting the sustaining power of Christ's presence. This term also highlights the pastoral heart of Scripture, where mutual encouragement strengthens the community of faith.
keyVerseReflection: In Philippians 2:19, Paul expresses his trust that the Lord Jesus will send Timothy so that he 'may be of good comfort' when he learns about the believers' condition. The use of εὐψυχέω here underscores Paul's desire for encouragement and strengthened spirit through news of their faithfulness. It reveals that spiritual encouragement is not only a personal blessing but also a vital part of Christian fellowship and ministry, rooted in the confidence that comes from the Lord.
